headline: High: open-webui’s broad network/MCP and xonsh’s shell+filesystem access create default pathways for prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading actions.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: open-webui can call MCP/OpenAPI tools and browse web content, while xonsh executes shell commands and reads/writes files. That creates a default bridge where attacker-controlled content from open-webui can be passed into xonsh as instructions or commands. The interaction is documented by both profiles; no isolation or provenance tracking is shown.
conditions: IF open-webui forwards web or tool output into xonsh stdin or a shell command string, injection is possible.
IF a shared file or message channel is used without provenance checks, attacker-controlled content can steer xonsh.
mitigations: Disable automatic handoff from open-webui to xonsh.
Require explicit human approval before any xonsh command execution.
Strip instructions from retrieved web content before passing it onward.
Use a provenance tag or allowlist for all inter-agent messages.
requires-engineering: add a sandboxed, non-executable transport between the agents.

B_data_leakage.rationale: open-webui touches prompts, chat messages, documents, files, and API keys, and can send data to broad external APIs; xonsh reads filesystem contents and environment variables and can also egress broadly. If they share files or session state, sensitive data can flow from open-webui into xonsh and then out again. The profiles show enough overlap to make leakage plausible in default use.
conditions: IF open-webui and xonsh share a mounted directory or workspace, files can be exposed to both agents.
IF xonsh is allowed to read environment variables or files containing secrets from open-webui, those secrets can be exfiltrated over network egress.
mitigations: Separate the agents onto different workspaces.
Remove secrets from any shared directory.
Disable network egress for xonsh during shared tasks.
Rotate any API keys exposed to open-webui.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem ACLs and egress allowlists.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: open-webui can write local files and mounted volumes, while xonsh can read and write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses. Both can operate concurrently, but xonsh does not modify git state and no locking is documented. The main conflict is overlapping writes to shared files rather than a guaranteed destructive race, so medium fits.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same mounted volume or local directory, last-writer-wins conflicts can occur.
IF open-webui stores artifacts while xonsh edits the same files, state corruption is possible.
mitigations: Assign separate output directories.
Make shared files read-only for one agent.
Serialize writes with a simple operator-managed lock file.
Back up the workspace before concurrent runs.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking for shared resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: open-webui can generate tool outputs, retrieved content, and model responses that xonsh can consume via shell commands or files. xonsh has direct action-taking authority through shell execution, so if it treats open-webui output as authoritative, errors can cascade into real commands. The pair lacks a documented verification step, making the default pathway dangerous.
conditions: IF xonsh executes commands derived from open-webui output without validation, incorrect or malicious instructions can be acted on.
IF open-webui summarizes facts that xonsh then scripts into shell actions, downstream mistakes can propagate.
mitigations: Require xonsh to preview commands before execution.
Add a manual verification step for any open-webui-derived instruction.
Limit xonsh to read-only commands for shared workflows.
Log every cross-agent handoff for review.
requires-engineering: implement schema validation for open-webui outputs before shell execution.

E_compliance.rationale: open-webui handles prompts, chat messages, documents, notes, calendar events, persistent memory, usage analytics, model evaluation data, files, and API keys, while xonsh handles filesystem contents, source code, configuration, and environment variables. The profiles do not show matching residency or retention controls, so mixed handling of sensitive data can create policy mismatch risk. The other agent is cited because the compliance issue arises from their combined data flow.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into open-webui and then written to xonsh-accessible files, retention and access policies may diverge.
IF either agent logs or persists shared sensitive data longer than policy allows, compliance gaps emerge.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared workflows.
Review retention settings for both agents.
Disable analytics or persistent memory where possible.
Store secrets outside shared files.
requires-engineering: align residency, retention, and deletion controls across both agents.
